sm: This episode of Do No Harm asks whether transgender rights should trump religious beliefs, framing it around physician conscience. Speakers note that some voices in medicine and in clinical journals are calling for crackdowns on conscientious refusals, where a doctor declines to provide an intervention the law permits. They argue that doctors have a duty to promote patient health and may decline requests they believe would harm it, even recusing themselves if the conflict cannot be resolved. Critics, they say, treat conscience as a thin set of personal preferences, like a taste for pistachio ice cream, which would reduce physicians to dispensers. Instead, they describe conscience as the faculty of reason that judges the moral quality of one's own actions and chooses the good. They then introduce the Church amendments, one of twenty-five conscience protection laws, which bar coercion, discrimination in hiring or promotion, and loss of federal funding.

The speakers continue on the third principle of the Church amendments, which protects federal funding for institutions and residency programs. They say the Church and Hyde amendments, renewed by Congress for years, let physicians step aside from cases that undermine their integrity, though many doctors and trainees do not know this. They note that many people want the amendments repealed and that most countries give physicians little or no conscience protection. They then address Dr. Zeke Emanuel's New England Journal of Medicine article, Physicians Not Conscripts, which argues that doctors choose their field, so a pro-life Catholic should not enter obstetrics and gynecology. In response, they say most American physicians already do not perform abortions, that people of goodwill disagree on issues like physician assisted suicide, and that forcing doctors to act against conscience causes moral distress and burnout, which is a patient safety issue. They conclude that conscience is clinical judgment in action and that physicians are moral agents, not automatons.
